What does "you can catch more flies with honey" mean? (Idioms in English, idioms explained)

When we arrange for someone else to do something for us — paint a room, fix a car, alter a dress — English uses a special structure called the causative. This conversation between two friends catching up over brunch is full of it.

The Causative English Listening Exercise (B2)

Aisha has just moved into a new apartment and tells Priya everything she arranged to get done — from painters to plumbers. Listen for the causative structure: have/get + something + done.

Pre-Listening

Matching Exercise ⭐

Before you listen, match each word or phrase with its correct meaning.

1-b, 2-e, 3-f, 4-c, 5-a, 6-d

While Listening

Listening and Answers to Focus Question ⭐⭐

Do the following task:

  • As you listen, count how many different services Aisha had done to her apartment, and note what she still needs to arrange.

Priya: The apartment looks amazing, Aisha! Did you do all of this yourself?

Aisha: Not quite! I had the whole apartment painted last month — I found a great crew on Angi. And I got the kitchen cabinets replaced at the same time.

Priya: I love those floors! Are they new?

Aisha: Yes! I had hardwood floors installed throughout. It was expensive but worth every penny. I also got the windows cleaned professionally — they were filthy when I moved in.

Priya: Smart! I need to have my car serviced — it’s been making a strange noise. And I want to get my sofa reupholstered — it’s still a great frame, but the fabric is worn out.

Aisha: Oh, that’s such a good idea instead of buying new! I had my grandmother’s dining table restored last year — it looks brand new now. Where do you have your car serviced usually?

Priya: There’s a great place on Michigan Avenue. They also do tires — I had four new tires fitted there last winter. And the best part — they get it washed and vacuumed while you wait!

Multiple Choice Exercise ⭐⭐

Choose the correct answer for each question.

  1. Who painted Aisha’s apartment?
    a) Aisha herself
    b) A hired crew
    c) Priya
    d) Nobody; it’s still unpainted
  2. What did Aisha have installed throughout the apartment?
    a) New windows
    b) New cabinets
    c) Hardwood floors
    d) A new sofa
  3. Why does Aisha need to have her car serviced?
    a) It won’t start
    b) It’s making a strange noise
    c) The tires are flat
    d) It needs to be painted
  4. What does Aisha want to do with her sofa?
    a) Sell it
    b) Throw it away
    c) Get it reupholstered
    d) Paint it
  5. Whose dining table did Aisha have restored?
    a) Priya’s
    b) Her own, bought new
    c) Her grandmother’s
    d) A neighbor’s
  6. What extra service does the garage provide with new tires?
    a) Free coffee
    b) A car wash and vacuum
    c) A rental car
    d) A discount coupon
1-b, 2-c, 3-b, 4-c, 5-c, 6-b

Table Completion Exercise ⭐⭐

Complete the table below with the causative structure Aisha uses for each service, then click “Show Answers” to check.

SocialSciences

Apartment painted — had … painted
Kitchen cabinets replaced — got … replaced
Hardwood floors installed — had … installed
Windows cleaned — got … cleaned
Car serviced — need to have … serviced
Sofa reupholstered — want to get … reupholstered
Dining table restored — had … restored
Four new tires fitted — had … fitted

Post Listening

Follow-up ⭐⭐⭐

Now it’s your turn to practice what you heard.

  1. Writing: Write 3–4 sentences describing services you have had done recently (or need to have done), using the causative.
  2. Speaking: Tell a partner about something you had done to your home, car, or clothes, using “have/get something done.”
  3. Discussion question: Is it better to do home repairs yourself or pay someone else to do them? Why?
  4. Transfer activity: Using the same causative patterns from the conversation, write a sentence for each person below describing what they had done.

Example: 1. Marcus had his roof repaired.

2. Fatima had her wedding dress altered.
3. Diego had his laptop screen fixed.

Quick Recap

Here’s what you practiced in this activity:

  • Using have + something + done to talk about a service arranged for you: “I had the apartment painted.”
  • Using get + something + done as a more informal alternative: “I got the cabinets replaced.”
  • Combining the causative with modals and other verb forms: “I need to have my car serviced,” “I want to get my sofa reupholstered.”

The Causative

Note: The causative is different from the passive. Compare: “The house was painted” (passive — we don’t know or care who arranged it) vs. “I had the house painted” (causative — I arranged for it to happen).

SocialSciences

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the causative form in English?

The causative (have/get + object + past participle) is used when you arrange for someone else to do something for you, rather than doing it yourself — for example, “I had my car serviced” means someone else serviced it at your request.

What’s the difference between “have something done” and “get something done”?

They mean the same thing, but “get something done” is more informal and common in everyday speech, while “have something done” is slightly more neutral or formal. Both are correct and widely used.

Is the causative the same as the passive voice?

No. The passive (“The car was serviced”) simply describes what happened to something, without focus on who arranged it. The causative (“I had the car serviced”) specifically shows that the subject arranged for the action to be done.

Can you use the causative with modals like need to or want to?

Yes. You can combine the causative with other verbs and modals, as in “I need to have my car serviced” or “I want to get my sofa reupholstered.” The causative structure itself doesn’t change.

How can I practice the causative structure?

Think about services you’ve recently arranged — a haircut, a repair, cleaning — and describe them using “had/got + something + past participle.” Practicing with your own real-life examples makes the structure much easier to remember.
